ja: だいはちじゅういちかい

p.src: Now, after Yingchun had gone back, Lady Xing behaved as though nothing had happened. Lady Wang, however, having raised the girl, was deeply grieved and sighed to herself for some time in her room. Just then Baoyu came to pay his respects. Seeing what looked like traces of tears on Lady Wang's face, he dared not sit down and merely stood beside her. Only when Lady Wang told him to sit did Baoyu edge onto the kang and take a place beside her. Lady Wang saw him staring blankly, as though he wanted to speak but could not bring himself to do so, and asked, “Why are you looking so dazed again?” “It is nothing in particular,” Baoyu replied. “But after hearing yesterday about what Second Sister has been going through, I truly cannot bear it for her. Though I dared not tell Grandmother, I have been unable to sleep these past two nights. How could a daughter of a family like ours endure such humiliation? Besides, Second Sister is the meekest of people and has never known how to quarrel with anyone. Yet of all men she had to encounter that heartless brute, who understands nothing at all of a woman's suffering.” As he spoke, tears nearly fell from his eyes. “There is nothing to be done about it,” said Lady Wang. As the saying goes, ‘A married daughter is water poured away.’ What can I possibly do?” Baoyu said, “Last night I thought of a plan. Let us simply report the matter to Grandmother and bring Second Sister home. She can live at Purple Caltrop Isle again, and all of us sisters and brothers can eat and play together as before, so that she need no longer suffer at the hands of that scoundrel of the Sun family. When he comes to fetch her, we shall flatly refuse to let her go. If he comes a hundred times, we shall keep her a hundred times and say only that it is Grandmother's wish. Would that not be splendid?” Lady Wang was both amused and vexed when she heard this. “You are having another of your foolish fits! What nonsense are you talking? Every girl must eventually leave her family and marry into another household. Her own family cannot look after her there; she can only trust to her fate. If she fares well, all is well, and if she fares badly, nothing can be done. Have you never heard people say, ‘Marry a cock and follow the cock; marry a dog and follow the dog’? Not everyone can become an Imperial Consort like your Eldest Sister. Besides, your Second Sister is a new bride, and young Master Sun is still a young man. Each has a temper of their own, and when two people have only just come together, some friction is natural. After a few years, when they have learned each other's ways and had sons and daughters, matters will improve. You are absolutely forbidden to breathe a single word of this before Grandmother. If I learn that you have, I shall not let you off. Now go and attend to your own affairs. Do not stay here talking nonsense.”

p.src: After this rebuke, Baoyu dared not say another word. He sat for a while, then came out looking utterly dejected. His heart was full of pent-up misery with nowhere to vent it. He walked into the garden and headed straight for the Naiad's House.

p.src: The moment he entered, he burst into loud sobs. Daiyu had just finished washing and dressing. The sight of Baoyu in such a state gave her a start, and she asked, “What has happened? Who have you quarreled with?” She asked him several times in succession. Baoyu lowered his head and collapsed over the table, sobbing so hard that he could not speak. Daiyu sat in her chair staring at him in bewilderment. After a while she asked, “Tell me plainly: has someone else upset you, or have I offended you?” Baoyu waved his hand. “Neither, neither.” “Then why are you grieving so bitterly?” Daiyu asked. “I only think the sooner all of us die, the better,” said Baoyu. “There truly is no pleasure at all in being alive!” Daiyu was even more astonished to hear this. “What a thing to say! Have you truly gone mad?” “I have not gone mad,” said Baoyu. “If I tell you, you will not be able to help grieving either. You too saw the state Second Sister was in when she came back the other day, and heard everything she said. Why must people marry when they grow up? Why marry only to suffer so cruelly in another household? Do you remember when we first founded the Crab-Flower Club? We all composed poems and took turns as host. How lively it was then! Now Cousin Bao has gone home, even Xiangling cannot come over, and Second Sister has married and left us. Those few who truly understood one another are all scattered, and everything has come to this. I meant to tell Grandmother and ask her to bring Second Sister home, but Mother would not allow it. Instead she called me foolish and said I was talking nonsense, and I dared say no more. It has been scarcely any time at all, yet just look—the garden is already utterly changed. Who knows what it will be like after a few more years? The more I think about it, the more impossible it is not to feel wretched.” As Daiyu listened, her head gradually sank and her body slowly withdrew toward the kang. Without uttering a word, she gave a sigh, lay down, and turned her face toward the inner wall.

p.src: Zijuan had just brought in the tea and was wondering what had happened between them when she saw them like this. Just then Xiren arrived. Coming in and seeing Baoyu, she said, “So Second Master is here! Her Ladyship is asking for you. I thought this must be where you were.” Hearing that it was Xiren, Daiyu raised herself slightly and invited her to sit down. Both of Daiyu’s eyes were already red-rimmed from crying. Seeing this, Baoyu said, “Cousin, what I said just now was only foolish nonsense. You needn’t grieve over it. If you care about what I say, then you must take even better care of yourself. Rest for a while. Her Ladyship has sent for me, so I’ll go and see what she wants, then come straight back.” With that, he walked out. Xiren quietly asked Daiyu, “What happened between you two again?” Daiyu replied, “He was grieving over his second sister. As for me, my eyes were itching just now, so I rubbed them. It was nothing.” Xiren said nothing, but hurried out after Baoyu, and they all went their separate ways. Baoyu went to Grandmother Jia’s quarters, but she had already retired for her midday rest, so he had no choice but to return to Happy Red Court. Later that afternoon, Baoyu awoke from his nap. Feeling thoroughly bored, he casually picked up a book to read. When Xiren saw him reading, she hurried off to brew tea and wait upon him. As it happened, the book Baoyu had picked up was Ancient Music-Bureau Ballads. Leafing idly through it, he came upon Cao Mengde’s poem beginning, “Over wine, let us sing: how long is human life?” and felt an unexpected pang in his heart. He put that volume down and took up another. It contained writings from the Jin dynasty. After turning a few pages, he suddenly closed the book, propped his cheek in his hand, and sat there in a daze. Xiren brought the tea, and seeing him in this state, asked, “Why have you stopped reading again?” Baoyu did not answer. He took the tea, drank a sip, and set it down. Unable to make head or tail of it, Xiren could only stand beside him and stare at him blankly. Suddenly Baoyu stood up and muttered under his breath, “What a phrase—‘to roam beyond the bounds of the body’!” Xiren found this amusing, but did not dare question him. She could only advise, “If you don’t care for these books, why not go for a stroll in the Garden instead? It would keep you from brooding yourself ill.” Baoyu merely murmured assent and walked out, still lost in thought.

p.src: Presently he reached Drenched Blossoms Pavilion, where all he saw was a desolate scene, its occupants gone and its rooms empty. He went on to All-Spice Court, where the fragrant plants remained as before, but the doors and windows were tightly shut. Rounding Lotus Fragrance Pavilion, he saw in the distance several people leaning against the railing near Smartweed Bank, while a few little maids crouched on the ground looking for something. Baoyu crept quietly behind the artificial hill and listened. He heard one of them say, “Let’s see whether it comes back up or not.” The voice sounded like Li Wen’s. Another laughed and said, “There, it’s gone under. I knew it wouldn’t come back up.” This was Tanchun’s voice. Another said, “That’s right. Don’t move, sister; just wait. It is bound to come up.” Yet another exclaimed, “It’s up!” These last two voices belonged to Li Qi and Xing Xiuyan. Unable to resist, Baoyu picked up a small piece of brick and tossed it into the water. It landed with a great splash, startling all four of them. They cried in surprise, “Who is playing such a nasty trick? You gave us such a fright!” Laughing, Baoyu leapt straight out from behind the rockery and said, “You’re all having a fine time! Why didn’t you call me?” Tanchun said, “I knew it could be no one else; only Second Brother would be so mischievous. There’s nothing else for it—you must pay us back properly for our fish. A fish had just come up, and we were on the very point of catching it when you frightened it away.” Baoyu laughed. “You were amusing yourselves here without even looking for me. I ought to punish you instead.” They all laughed together for a while. Baoyu said, “Let’s all fish today and use it to divine who has the best luck. Whoever catches one will have good fortune this year, and whoever fails will have bad fortune. Who shall go first?” Tanchun offered the first turn to Li Wen, but Li Wen declined. Tanchun laughed. “In that case, I’ll fish first.” Turning to Baoyu, she added, “Second Brother, if you scare my fish away again, I won’t let you off.” Baoyu replied, “I only meant to startle you for fun before. Go ahead and fish now; I won’t disturb you.” Tanchun cast in the silken line. Before they had exchanged a dozen sentences, a little willow-leaf minnow swallowed the hook and pulled the float under. Tanchun jerked up the rod and flung the fish onto the ground, where it leapt and thrashed about. Shishu scrambled after it all over the ground, caught it in both hands, and placed it in a little porcelain jar filled with clean water. Tanchun handed the fishing rod to Li Wen. Li Wen lowered the rod too. No sooner did she feel the line twitch than she hurriedly lifted it, only to find the hook bare. She lowered it again. After quite some time, the line twitched once more, but when she raised it, the hook was still bare. Li Wen brought the hook up for a closer look and discovered that its point had bent inward.

p.src: Li Wen laughed. “No wonder you couldn't catch anything.” She hurriedly told Suyun to straighten the hook, put on a fresh worm, and secure the piece of reed above it. After she had lowered it for a while, she saw the piece of reed sink straight down. She swiftly pulled up the line and found she had caught a crucian carp about two inches long. Li Wen said with a smile, “Now you have a try, Brother Bao.” Baoyu said, “I may as well wait until Third Sister and Cousin Xing have fished.” Xiuyan, however, said nothing. Then Li Qi said, “You go first, Brother Bao.” As she spoke, a bubble rose on the surface of the water. Tanchun said, “There's no need for everyone to keep yielding. Look, all the fish are over by Third Sister. Third Sister had better hurry and fish.” Smiling, Li Qi took the rod, and sure enough, as soon as the float sank she caught one. Xiuyan then caught one as well and handed the rod back to Tanchun, who at last passed it to Baoyu. Baoyu said, “I intend to play Jiang Taigong.” He stepped down from the rocky ledge and sat beside the pond to fish, little knowing that when the fish saw his shadow in the water, they all fled elsewhere. Baoyu held the rod out and waited for ages, but the line did not stir in the least. Just as a fish came to the water's edge and blew bubbles, Baoyu gave the rod a flick and frightened it away again. Growing impatient, Baoyu said, “I am the most impatient of men, yet the fish insists on taking its time. What am I to do? Dear fish, come quickly! Do me a good turn, won't you?” At this, all four girls laughed. Before he had finished speaking, the line gave a slight twitch. Baoyu was beside himself with delight and jerked upward with all his strength. The rod struck the rock and broke in two, the line snapped, and no one knew where the hook had flown. Everyone laughed harder than ever. Tanchun said, “I have never seen anyone as rash as you.” While they were speaking, Sheyue came running up in a panic and said, “Second Master, the Old Lady is awake and says you are to come quickly.” All five of them started in alarm. Tanchun asked Sheyue, “What does the Old Lady want Second Brother for?” Sheyue replied, “I don't know either. I only heard that something had caused a terrible commotion and that Baoyu was to be called in and questioned. Second Mistress Lian is to investigate it with him as well.” Baoyu was so frightened that he stood dazed for a while, then said, “I wonder which maid has run into trouble this time.” Tanchun said, “We don't know what has happened. Second Brother, hurry along, and as soon as you hear anything, have Sheyue come and tell us.” With that, she left together with Li Wen, Li Qi, and Xiuyan.

p.src: Baoyu went to Grandmother Jia's rooms, where he found Lady Wang keeping her company over a game of cards. Seeing that nothing was amiss, Baoyu's mind was half relieved. When Grandmother Jia saw him come in, she asked, “When you fell seriously ill the year before last, you were finally cured thanks to a mad monk and a lame Taoist. While you were ill, what did it feel like to you?” Baoyu thought for a while and replied, “I remember that when the illness struck, I had been standing there perfectly well when it suddenly felt as though someone behind me had dealt me a blow squarely on the head. The pain made everything go black before my eyes, and I saw the whole room filled with hideous blue-faced, tusked demons brandishing knives and clubs. When I lay down on the kang, it felt as though several iron bands had been clamped around my head. After that, the pain grew so severe that I knew nothing at all. When I began to recover, I remember a flood of golden light shining from the main hall straight into my room. All those demons ran to hide from it and then vanished. My head stopped hurting, and my mind cleared as well.” Grandmother Jia said to Lady Wang, “That is more or less the same sort of thing.”

p.src: As they spoke, Xifeng came in too. After paying her respects to Grandmother Jia, she turned and greeted Lady Wang, then asked, “What did you wish to ask me, Old Ancestress?” Grandmother Jia said, “When that evil illness seized you the year before last, do you still remember what it was like?” Xifeng laughed. “I do not remember it very clearly. I only felt that I had no control over my own body, as though ghosts and demons were dragging me about and would not be satisfied until I had killed someone. Whatever came to hand I seized, and whatever I saw I tried to kill. I knew perfectly well that I was exhausted, yet I could not stop my hands.” Grandmother Jia asked, “Do you remember when you recovered?” Xifeng replied, “When I recovered, it seemed as though someone in the air had spoken a few words, but I cannot remember what was said.” Grandmother Jia said, “Then it truly must have been her. The condition of you two during your illness was exactly as you have just described. That old wretch was so wicked, and Baoyu was a fool to acknowledge her as his godmother. It was that monk and the Taoist—Amitabha Buddha!—who truly saved Baoyu’s life, yet we never repaid them.” Xifeng asked, “What made you think of our illness, Old Madam?” Grandmother Jia said, “Ask your mistress. I cannot be bothered to tell it.” Lady Wang said, “Just now the Master came in and told us that Baoyu’s godmother was nothing but a vile fraud, a practitioner of black magic and heretical arts. Her crimes have now come to light. She was seized by the Embroidered Uniform Guard and sent to the Ministry of Justice prison, where she is to be tried on a capital charge. Someone denounced her a few days ago. A man named Pan Sanbao had a house that he wished to sell to the pawnshop diagonally opposite. The price of the house had already been raised severalfold, but Pan Sanbao demanded still more, and the pawnshop naturally refused. So Pan Sanbao bribed that old wretch. She often visited the pawnshop, and was on intimate terms with all the women of the household. She worked a spell that made the proprietor’s wife fall prey to an evil illness, throwing the whole household into turmoil. Then she went there and claimed that she could cure the illness. She burned offerings of spirit-horse paper and ritual money, and sure enough it proved effective. She also demanded more than ten taels of silver from the women of the household. But Heaven has eyes, and her crimes were destined to be exposed. One day, as she hurried home, she dropped a silk bundle. The people at the pawnshop picked it up and looked inside. It contained many paper figures and four pellets of highly fragrant incense. While they were still puzzling over it, the old wretch came back in search of the bundle. The people there seized her and searched her person. They found a box containing two naked demons, one male and one female, carved from ivory, together with seven vermilion embroidery needles. u.src: As they spoke, Xifeng came in too. After paying her respects to Grandmother Jia, she turned and greeted Lady Wang, then asked, “What did you wish to ask me, Old Ancestress?”
Grandmother Jia said, “When that evil illness seized you the year before last, do you still remember what it was like?”
Xifeng laughed. “I do not remember it very clearly.

I only felt that I had no control over my own body, as though ghosts and demons were dragging me about and would not be satisfied until I had killed someone. Whatever came to hand I seized, and whatever I saw I tried to kill.
I knew perfectly well that I was exhausted, yet I could not stop my hands.”
Grandmother Jia asked, “Do you remember when you recovered?”
Xifeng replied, “When I recovered, it seemed as though someone in the air had spoken a few words, but I cannot remember what was said.”
Grandmother Jia said, “Then it truly must have been her.
The condition of you two during your illness was exactly as you have just described.
That old wretch was so wicked, and Baoyu was a fool to acknowledge her as his godmother.
It was that monk and the Taoist—Amitabha Buddha!—who truly saved Baoyu’s life, yet we never repaid them.”
Xifeng asked, “What made you think of our illness, Old Madam?”
Grandmother Jia said, “Ask your mistress. I cannot be bothered to tell it.”
Lady Wang said, “Just now the Master came in and told us that Baoyu’s godmother was nothing but a vile fraud, a practitioner of black magic and heretical arts.

Her crimes have now come to light. She was seized by the Embroidered Uniform Guard and sent to the Ministry of Justice prison, where she is to be tried on a capital charge. Someone denounced her a few days ago.
A man named Pan Sanbao had a house that he wished to sell to the pawnshop diagonally opposite.
The price of the house had already been raised severalfold, but Pan Sanbao demanded still more, and the pawnshop naturally refused.
So Pan Sanbao bribed that old wretch. She often visited the pawnshop, and was on intimate terms with all the women of the household.
She worked a spell that made the proprietor’s wife fall prey to an evil illness, throwing the whole household into turmoil.
Then she went there and claimed that she could cure the illness. She burned offerings of spirit-horse paper and ritual money, and sure enough it proved effective.
She also demanded more than ten taels of silver from the women of the household.
But Heaven has eyes, and her crimes were destined to be exposed.

The people at the pawnshop picked it up and looked inside. It contained many paper figures and four pellets of highly fragrant incense.
While they were still puzzling over it, the old wretch came back in search of the bundle.
The people there seized her and searched her person. They found a box containing two naked demons, one male and one female, carved from ivory, together with seven vermilion embroidery needles.
She was immediately sent to the Embroidered Uniform Guard, where interrogation uncovered many secret affairs involving the wives and daughters of officials and wealthy families.

p.src: The military authorities were therefore notified, and when her house was searched, a great many clay images of baleful spirits and several boxes of bewitching incense were discovered. In an empty room behind the kang hung a Seven-Star Lamp. Beneath it were several straw figures: some wore bands around their heads, some had nails driven through their chests, and some had chains fastened around their necks. There were countless paper figures in a cupboard, and beneath them several small account books recording that a certain household had tested the magic and that so much silver remained to be collected. The oil money and shares of incense offerings she had received from other households were beyond counting. Xifeng said, “She must certainly have been behind our illness. I remember that after we recovered, that old witch visited Concubine Zhao several times to demand silver from her. Whenever she saw me, her face changed color and her eyes became as dark and furtive as a black hen’s. At the time I suspected her more than once, but could never discover the reason. Now that we speak of it, I see there was a reason for everything. Still, since I manage the household here, I naturally incur people’s resentment, so it is hardly surprising that someone should seek to harm me. But what grudge could anyone have against Baoyu, that they could bring themselves to deal him such a vicious blow?” Grandmother Jia said, “How do we know it was not because I doted on Baoyu and neglected Huan, causing someone to poison you both?” Lady Wang said, “That old woman has already been convicted, and we certainly cannot bring her here to confront anyone. Without a witness to confront her, Concubine Zhao would never admit it. Besides, the matter is serious, and if it became public it would reflect badly on us. Let her reap what she has sown; sooner or later she will expose herself.” Grandmother Jia said, “What you say is right. In a matter like this, without direct testimony it is difficult to be certain. But the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see the truth clearly. And are those two of ours now in any way inferior to anyone else? Enough. It is all in the past, so you need not speak of it again, Xifeng. Today you and your mistress shall both dine here with me before you go back.” She then ordered Yuanyang, Hupo, and the others to have the meal served. Xifeng hastily laughed and said, “Why should the Old Ancestress trouble herself over such things!” Lady Wang laughed as well. Several married servants were waiting outside. Xifeng promptly told a young maid to order the meal: “The mistress and I will both dine with the Old Madam.” As she spoke, Yuchuan came over and said to Lady Wang, “The Master is looking for something. He asks that, after you have attended the Old Madam through her meal, you go and find it yourself.” Grandmother Jia said, “Go along. Your master may well have some urgent business.” Lady Wang assented, left Xifeng behind to attend Grandmother Jia, and withdrew.

p.src: Returning to her room, she chatted for a while with Jia Zheng and took out the things she had found. Jia Zheng then asked, “Ying'er has gone back already. How is she faring in the Sun household?” Lady Wang replied, “Poor Ying was full of tears. She says our son-in-law Sun is unbearably brutal and overbearing.” She then repeated everything Yingchun had told her. Jia Zheng sighed. “I knew from the start it was not a suitable match, but the Elder Master had already settled it, so there was nothing I could do. Poor Ying will simply have to endure some hardship.” Lady Wang said, “She is still a new bride. We can only hope he will treat her better in time.” As she spoke, she gave a sudden chuckle. “What are you laughing at?” asked Jia Zheng. Lady Wang replied, “I was laughing at Baoyu. Early this morning he came here especially to see me and said nothing but childish things.” “What did he say?” asked Jia Zheng. Smiling, Lady Wang repeated what Baoyu had said. Jia Zheng could not help laughing either. Then he said, “Now that you mention Baoyu, I have just remembered something. It will not do to leave that boy idling in the Garden every day. If a daughter proves unpromising, she will eventually belong to another family; but if a son proves useless, the consequences are grave indeed. The other day someone recommended a tutor to me, a southerner of excellent learning and character. But southerners are generally the mildest-tempered of tutors, while the boys in our city are all wild enough to kick up heaven and turn wells upside down. They have plenty of sly cleverness and will bluff their way through whenever they can; they are brazen too. If the tutor cannot bring himself to shame them, but spends every day coaxing them like pampered young masters, their time will merely be wasted. That is why our forebears would not engage an outside tutor. They chose instead an older man of some learning from within the clan to take charge of the family school. Great-uncle Ru's learning may be only middling, but he can at least keep these boys under control and will not muddle his way through his duties. I do not think it wise for Baoyu to remain idle. We had better send him back to study at the family school.” Lady Wang replied, “You are quite right, sir. Since you left to take up your provincial appointment, his frequent illnesses have caused him to lose several years. For the present, it would certainly do him good to review his lessons at the family school.” Jia Zheng nodded, and after some further casual conversation, the matter was dropped.

p.src: Now the next morning, after Baoyu had risen and finished washing and dressing, the pages promptly sent in word: “The Master wishes to speak with Second Master Bao.” Baoyu hurriedly straightened his clothes, went to Jia Zheng's study, paid his respects, and stood waiting. Jia Zheng asked, “What lessons have you been working on lately? You have written a few compositions, perhaps, but they hardly amount to anything. From what I have seen of you lately, you have grown even more idle and undisciplined than you were a few years ago. Moreover, I am constantly hearing that you plead illness to avoid your studies. Now you have made a fine recovery, yet I hear that every day you frolic and laugh with your sisters in the Garden, and even romp about with the maids, while forever putting your proper duties out of mind. Even the few lines of verse you compose are nothing remarkable. What is there to be proud of? When it comes to the civil examinations and official selection, prose essays are what matter; yet you have put no effort whatsoever into them. Mark my words: from this day forward, you are forbidden to compose poems or antithetical couplets. You are to devote yourself solely to the study of the eight-legged essay. I give you one year. If you show no improvement at all, you need study no more—and I, for my part, want no son like you.” He then summoned Li Gui and said, “Early tomorrow morning, have Beiming accompany Baoyu to gather the books he ought to study. Bring them all here for me to inspect, and I shall personally escort him to the family school.” Then he barked at Baoyu, “Go! Come to see me early tomorrow morning.” On hearing this, Baoyu stood for a long while without finding a single word to answer, and then returned to Happy Red Court.

p.src: Aroma had been anxiously waiting for news; when she heard that his books were to be fetched, she was actually pleased. Baoyu alone insisted that someone immediately inform Grandmother Jia, hoping she would intervene. When Grandmother Jia received the message, she had Baoyu summoned and told him, “Set your mind at ease and go for now. Do not make your father angry. If anything proves too hard for you, you have me to rely on.” Baoyu had no choice but to return and instruct the maids, “Wake me very early tomorrow. Father will be waiting to take me to the family school.” Aroma and the others agreed, and she and Musk took turns staying awake throughout the night.

p.src: Early the next morning, Aroma woke Baoyu, helped him wash and change his clothes, and sent a young maid to tell Beiming to wait at the inner gate with the books and other things. After Aroma had urged him twice more, Baoyu had no choice but to leave and make his way to Jia Zheng's study. First he asked, “Has Father come yet?” A page in the study replied, “A literary gentleman came just now to ask the Master for instructions. Word came from inside that the Master was washing and dressing, so the gentleman was told to wait outside.” Hearing this, Baoyu felt somewhat reassured and hurried over to Jia Zheng's quarters. Just then Jia Zheng sent someone to summon him, and Baoyu followed the messenger inside. Jia Zheng naturally gave him several more admonitions, then took Baoyu into the carriage. With Beiming carrying the books, they proceeded straight to the family school.

p.src: Someone had already hurried ahead to inform Dai-ru, “The master has arrived.” Dai-ru rose to his feet, but Jia Zheng had already entered and paid his respects to him. Dai-ru took his hand and exchanged greetings with him, then asked, “Has the old lady been well lately?” Baoyu also came forward and paid his respects. Jia Zheng remained standing until Dai-ru had taken his seat, and only then sat down himself. Jia Zheng said, “I have brought him here myself today because I have a favor to ask of you. The boy is no longer so young; he must at last learn the examination studies expected of a grown man, for only thus can he establish himself and make a name for the rest of his life. At present he does nothing at home but fool around with the other children. Though he knows a few lines of verse, they are merely wild and random effusions; even at their best, they concern no more than winds, clouds, moonlight, and dew, and have nothing whatever to do with the serious business of his life.” Dai-ru said, “He is presentable enough in appearance and not lacking in intelligence. The reason he does not study is simply that his mind is unruly and he is addicted to play. There is nothing wrong with learning poetry, but it will not be too late to take it up after he has attained success.” “Precisely,” said Jia Zheng. For now, I ask only that he read the classics, expound them, and write essays. If he should refuse instruction, I beg you, venerable sir, to discipline him in earnest, lest his schooling prove an empty name and his whole life be wasted for nothing.” When he had finished speaking, he rose and bowed once more; then, after exchanging some casual remarks, he took his leave. Dai-ru accompanied him to the entrance and said, “Please convey my respects and good wishes to the old lady.” Jia Zheng promised that he would, then boarded his carriage and departed.

p.src: Dai-ru turned and went back inside. He saw that a small rosewood desk had been set for Baoyu by the window in the southwest corner, with two sets of old books and one slender volume of model essays piled to its right; Baoyu had told Beiming to put the paper, ink, brushes, and inkstone away in the drawer. Dai-ru said, “Baoyu, I heard that you were ill the other day. Have you fully recovered now?” Baoyu rose and replied, “I am completely recovered.” Dai-ru said, “As matters stand, it is time you applied yourself to your studies. Your father is most earnest in his wish to see you become a worthy man. Begin by going through all the books you studied before, starting from the very beginning. Each day, review your books early in the morning, practice calligraphy after breakfast, explain the classics at noon, and read the model essays several times. That will suffice.” Baoyu answered, “Yes.” As he turned and sat down, he could not help looking all around him. Several of the former pupils, such as Jinrong, were no longer there, while a few younger boys had been added, all of them exceptionally coarse and vulgar. Suddenly he thought of Qin Zhong. There was no one now to keep him company or exchange a heartfelt word with him. He felt desolate and unhappy, but dared not utter a sound and could only bury his gloom in his books. Dai-ru told Baoyu, “Since this is your first day, I shall let you go home early. Tomorrow you will have to expound the classics. But you are not altogether dull-witted, so tomorrow I shall first have you explain a chapter or two for me. I want to see how your recent studies have progressed, so that I may know precisely what level you have reached.” At these words, Baoyu’s heart began to pound wildly. To learn how his exposition went the next day, listen to the explanation in the following chapter.
